title: Brill Pays
passages:
Rhea cut the flatbed's engine forty meters short of Marrow Cut's door plate. The exhaust ticked as it cooled. She climbed down with Teodoro's written order folded in her hand and walked to the concrete pad where Dray stood planted, hands in his coat.

"Reader two logged eleven canisters at Culvert Nine's jaw as Anza salvage," Rhea said, holding out the paper. "That's an order, not a request. My node is sending a flatbed to haul them back."

Dray didn't take it. He looked at the shed behind him, then at her flatbed. "A blank rig is a parts pile," he said. "A rig lives while a living name is wired to its crew plate. The cans in that jaw have no plate. No name. No one to answer for them."

"They have a log," Rhea said. "And my brother is breathing on Anza mains compressor power because of those cans. I don't trade names. I haul cargo."

Dray shifted his weight. "I mean to buy them with a name. One name, wired to plate 4217 — Rig Seven, dark eleven months — before two witnesses. Without it, nothing in this shed moves. Not the cans, not my rigs, not you."

Rhea looked past him at the shed door. She could see the dim glow of Amil's bench inside. She had trusted a truck's diagnostics more than a person's word her whole life. She trusted the reader's log more than Dray's book.

"Then you'll wait a long time," she said. "My flatbed's got fuel and no schedule."

She turned and walked back to the cab. The door plate rattled as she swung up into the seat. She dropped the order onto the dash and started the engine. The transmission whined into gear.

Dray shouted after her, "The reader's log doesn't feed a crew through winter!"

"It feeds my brother," Rhea said, and released the brake.

The flatbed lurched forward, tires spitting gravel. She aimed for the spur, the narrow track that ran back down to Culvert Nine's jaw. If she beat Dray there, she could slap Teodoro's order on the receiving plate and have Brill crank the jaw open before Dray could wire a name to anything.

In her side mirror, Rig Seven's headlight stayed dark inside the shed. Behind her, Dray's rig coughed to life, its own lamps sweeping across the yard. Her transponder blinked red on the dash. Teodoro's order wasn't worth the paper it was printed on if Dray was coming down the spur after her.

Rhea cut the engine at the receiving plate. The flatbed’s suspension sighed and settled. She stepped down with Teodoro’s order folded in her fist and walked to the steel jaw housing that ringed Culvert Nine’s unload clamp. The jaw was shut, dark around the blank rig’s nose, its hydraulic arm locked.

She slapped the paper against the housing. Metal on metal.

“Crank it,” she said. “Eleven canisters. Ten good, one spoiled. Anza salvage, logged at reader two. That’s an order, not a request.”

Brill came out from behind the pump station’s shadow, her coveralls greased at the knees. She didn’t touch the paper.

“A order isn’t a trade,” Brill said. “My jaw takes a matched seal. My shelf takes a name on steel. You got neither.”

“It’s Teodoro’s signature. Anza’s relay operator. Reader two logged the count.”

“Reader two’s been dead since the freeze,” Brill said. “It woke once, spit out a log for a blank rig, and went back to sleep. I don’t take ghost reads. I take trades. That’s the rule here, and I don’t break it for red lights or relay operators.”

Saul stepped out from the door plate, his hands in his pockets. He looked at the order, then at Rhea’s transponder blinking red on the dash.

“C9-047 was Miko Keres,” Saul said. “She burned her tickets and rubbed her ink off the steel. This manifest’s got dead names and one pencil scratch. A pencil name won’t hold wire or ink.”

“Ivo’s breathing on Anza mains compressor power because of those cans,” Rhea said. “Open the jaw.”

“Then Ivo should’ve been on steel,” Brill said. She planted her boots against the jaw’s arm. “Rule at C9: nothing out without a trade. Nothing in without a name on steel. You want my cans? Give me a name. Yours. Your brother’s. The one blinking red in your cab. I write it on the tally, I set the record against the trade, and I crank.”

Rhea’s fingers tightened on the order. “I don’t trade names.”

“Then you don’t eat,” Brill said. “Anza’s board is red. Resupply is frozen. Your signature on waste paper doesn’t feed my crew through winter. My storeroom feeds names on steel, and you ain’t on it.”

Rhea looked back down the spur. Dust was rising in the headlights’ wash. Dray’s rig was cresting the bend, lamps cutting through the dark, seconds from pinning her against the jaw.

Brill pulled a stub of pencil from her coverall pocket and held it out. “Whose name?”

The headlights washed over Rhea’s back. Dray’s engine cut to idle. The exhaust ticked behind her.

Brill didn’t turn. “The jaw’s waiting. The trade’s waiting. Give me a name, or tell your brother to hold his breath.”

The exhaust ticked. Dray’s rig sat with its lamps sweeping the jaw housing, the blank rig’s nose dark inside the steel teeth. Miko stayed on the running board, one-twenty-seven chalked on her shoulder, her hands loose at her sides. She hadn’t spoken since she climbed up, and she didn’t look down at Rhea.

Dray climbed down from the cab. His coat was heavy at the shoulders, plate-wired at the sternum like every yard rider. He didn’t look at Rhea. He looked at the pencil still held out in Brill’s hand.

“Put that away,” Dray said. “You don’t trade with a pencil.”

Brill’s fingers closed around it. “I don’t trade with you at all.”

“I’m not offering a trade,” Dray said. “I’m stating a price. Plate 4217. Rig Seven. Dark eleven months. It stays a parts pile until a living name is wired to its crew plate before two witnesses.” He nodded at Saul, then at Brill. “You two are standing. That’s your witnesses.”

“And if nobody wires?” Rhea said.

“Then nothing in this shed moves. Not the cans in the jaw, not my rigs, not you. One name, wired loud and clean before two witnesses. That’s the rate. One can for the name.”

Rhea’s knuckles whitened on Teodoro’s order. “My brother’s name isn’t on that plate. Ivo’s breathing on Anza mains compressor power. He’s not cargo.”

“Then he’s not a name I can use,” Dray said. “I need a name with breath and a board. You want eleven cans, you bring me eleven names.”

Dray lifted a hand, not a wave, an indication. Miko on his deck, chalked one-twenty-seven, nameless.

“She’s got no name,” Dray said. “No badge. No steel. She rode as cargo, and cargo doesn’t eat unless it’s claimed. One-twenty-seven. She’s standing on my rig. She’s available.”

Miko’s fingers curled against the running board. She didn’t look at Rhea. She didn’t look at Brill. She looked at Dray, waiting to see if he meant it.

The exhaust ticked again. Behind Rhea, the flatbed’s transponder blinked red on the dash. Teodoro’s order was still folded in her fist, worthless against Dray’s book.

“Whose name?” Brill asked again, but her voice had gone quiet.

Dray didn’t answer her. He looked at Miko.
